questions.title: Which claimed advantage of beta-1 selective blockers is false
questions.question: Adrenergic beta-1 selective blockers offer the following advantages EXCEPT:

options.B: Less prone to produce cold hands and feet

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS an advantage). Sparing beta-2 receptors in the airways means less bronchospasm than with non-selective blockers.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS an advantage). Sparing beta-2-mediated vasodilation means less peripheral vasoconstriction, so fewer cold extremities.
explanations.C: Correct answer. Beta-1 selectivity is only RELATIVE, not absolute: at higher doses these agents also block beta-2 receptors, so the selectivity is lost. Claiming it is absolute is therefore the false statement and the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS an advantage). Sparing beta-2 receptors preserves adrenaline-driven glycogenolysis, so beta-1 selective agents are less likely to mask or prolong hypoglycaemia.

questions.learning_objective: State that beta-1 selectivity is relative and lost at high doses.

questions.title: Atropine substitute mismatched with its use
questions.question: Which of the following atropine substitutes is NOT matched correctly with its use?

explanations.A: Correct pairing (so not the answer). Hyoscine butylbromide is a poorly absorbed antimuscarinic antispasmodic used for abdominal colic.
explanations.B: Correct answer. This is the WRONG match: tiotropium is a long-acting inhaled antimuscarinic used as a bronchodilator in COPD and asthma, NOT for urinary incontinence (which is treated with uroselective antimuscarinics such as tolterodine or solifenacin). Pairing tiotropium with incontinence is therefore incorrect.
explanations.C: Correct pairing (so not the answer). Short-acting tropicamide is used to dilate the pupil for fundus examination.
explanations.D: Correct pairing (so not the answer). Benztropine, a central antimuscarinic, is used in Parkinsonism.

questions.learning_objective: Match antimuscarinic subtypes to their organ-selective uses and recognise tiotropium as an airway, not bladder, drug.

questions.title: Agent to confirm a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis
questions.question: A 44-year-old man has intermittent fatigue and drooping eyelids. Administration of which of the following agents is most appropriate to confirm a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adrenaline is a sympathomimetic with no role in diagnosing myasthenia gravis.
explanations.B: Correct. Edrophonium is an ultra-short-acting anticholinesterase; in the Tensilon test it transiently raises acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, and a prompt but brief improvement in muscle strength (for example resolution of ptosis) confirms myasthenia gravis. Its very short duration makes it ideal for a rapid diagnostic challenge. That is why it is the appropriate confirmatory agent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bethanechol is a direct muscarinic agonist acting on smooth muscle, not a diagnostic anticholinesterase for the neuromuscular junction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Physostigmine is a longer-acting anticholinesterase used therapeutically; edrophonium's brevity makes it the preferred diagnostic agent.

questions.learning_objective: Identify edrophonium as the short-acting anticholinesterase used to confirm myasthenia gravis (Tensilon test).

questions.title: Calculating the apparent volume of distribution
questions.question: A drug given as a 200 mg single intravenous dose produces a peak plasma concentration of 0.02 mg/ml. The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This does not satisfy Vd = dose / plasma concentration for the given figures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 4 litres would require a plasma concentration of 0.05 mg/ml, which is not the case here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 5 litres would require a concentration of 0.04 mg/ml, not 0.02 mg/ml.
explanations.D: Correct. The apparent volume of distribution is Vd = dose / plasma concentration. Here Vd = 200 mg / 0.02 mg per ml = 10 000 ml = 10 litres. This is the only option consistent with the definition, so the answer is 10 litres.

questions.learning_objective: Calculate the apparent volume of distribution as dose divided by plasma concentration.

questions.title: Calculating a maintenance infusion rate
questions.question: It is desired to maintain a plasma concentration of 0.2 g/L of an antibiotic. Plasma clearance equals 6 L/hour. Calculate the maintenance infusion rate:

explanations.A: Correct. At steady state the maintenance infusion rate equals target concentration multiplied by clearance: rate = Css × CL = 0.2 g/L × 6 L/hour = 1.2 g/hour. This balances the amount cleared per hour, so the answer is 1.2 g/hour.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 2.4 g/hour is twice the required rate and would drive the concentration above target.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 3 g/hour does not equal Css × CL for these values.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 5 g/hour greatly exceeds the product of concentration and clearance.

questions.learning_objective: Calculate a maintenance infusion rate as target concentration multiplied by clearance.

questions.title: Time to reach steady-state plasma concentration
questions.question: The half-life of a drug is about 6 hours. Approximately how long will it take for blood levels to reach a steady (plateau) concentration on regular dosing?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 12 hours is only two half-lives, giving about 75% of steady state, which is not yet the plateau.
explanations.B: Correct. Steady state is reached after roughly four to five half-lives. With a half-life of 6 hours, four half-lives is about 24 hours (approximately 94% of steady state), which is the best approximation of the plateau among the options. Hence about 24 hours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 48 hours is eight half-lives, far beyond the time actually needed to plateau.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 4 days is much longer than the four to five half-lives required.

questions.learning_objective: State that steady state is reached after about four to five half-lives.
